idiom_name: wrapper struct implementing the Subject interface (held or embedded target)
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance and does not need it: a proxy is a struct whose method set implements the same interface as the subject and whose methods forward to a held (or embedded) target, so substitution is structural and the compiler enforces the contract. Embedding the interface gives free forwarding for methods you do not override, but an embedded interface that is never set panics on first use, so a named field plus explicit methods is the safer default for a proxy with a policy. The standard library has no generic object proxy; net/http/httputil.ReverseProxy is the ready-made realization for the network-proxy kind, with Director/ModifyResponse/ErrorHandler as its policy hooks.
pitfalls: A nil interface value and an interface holding a typed nil pointer behave differently: forwarding to an unset target either panics with a confusing message or silently no-ops.
Lazy state must be guarded (sync.Once/sync.OnceValues or a mutex); a proxy struct with a mutex must never be copied by value, and `go vet` flags it.
Clients that accept a concrete struct instead of the interface cannot be given the proxy - define the Subject as an interface before adding the proxy.
Embedding the interface exposes the whole method set and lets callers see promoted methods you did not intend to intercept; embed only when the forwarding is genuinely transparent.
